'use client'

import type { ComponentProps, ReactNode, Ref } from 'react'
import { Toggle } from '@base-ui/react/toggle'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import { Button, type ButtonProps } from './Button'
import styles from './ToggleButton.module.css'

interface ToggleButtonBaseProps
  extends Omit<ComponentProps<'button'>, 'ref' | 'value' | 'defaultValue' | 'onChange'> {
  // Always a <button> (Button itself may be an <a>, hence its wider type).
  ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement>
  /** Colour of the pressed state. Unpressed is always neutral. */
  variant?: ButtonProps['variant']
  /** Style of the pressed state. */
  appearance?: ButtonProps['appearance']
  size?: ButtonProps['size']
  startIcon?: ReactNode
  endIcon?: ReactNode
  isLoading?: boolean
  isFullWidth?: boolean
  /** Controlled pressed state (the spec's `isSelected`). */
  pressed?: boolean
  defaultPressed?: boolean
  /** Base UI's second argument (event details) is dropped: nothing here needs it. */
  onPressedChange?: (pressed: boolean) => void
  /** Identifies the toggle inside a group. */
  value?: string
}

/** An icon-only toggle has no text to name it, so `aria-label` is required. */
export type ToggleButtonProps =
  | (ToggleButtonBaseProps & { isIconOnly?: false })
  | (ToggleButtonBaseProps & { isIconOnly: true; 'aria-label': string })

export function ToggleButton({
  variant = 'primary',
  appearance = 'contained',
  size,
  startIcon,
  endIcon,
  isLoading,
  isFullWidth,
  isIconOnly,
  pressed,
  defaultPressed,
  onPressedChange,
  disabled,
  className,
  children,
  ...props
}: ToggleButtonProps) {
  return (
    <Toggle
      {...props}
      pressed={pressed}
      defaultPressed={defaultPressed}
      onPressedChange={onPressedChange && ((next) => onPressedChange(next))}
      disabled={disabled}
      render={(toggleProps, state) => {
        const buttonProps = {
          ...toggleProps,
          // Off is the same neutral button whatever the pressed style is, so
          // "on" is always the one that stands out.
          variant: state.pressed ? variant : 'secondary',
          appearance: state.pressed ? appearance : appearance === 'ghost' ? 'ghost' : 'outlined',
          size,
          startIcon,
          endIcon,
          isLoading,
          isFullWidth,
          // Its aria-label reached Toggle with the other props and comes back
          // in toggleProps, which is what Button's icon-only type asks for.
          isIconOnly,
          // A disabled ButtonGroup disables its toggles through state.
          disabled: state.disabled,
          className: cn(state.pressed && appearance !== 'contained' && styles.tinted, className),
          children,
        } as ButtonProps
        return <Button {...buttonProps} />
      }}
    />
  )
}

# Toggle Button A button that stays pressed: bold on or off, following or not, a filter ap...

# Toggle Button

<DocTabs>
<DocTab value="overview">

A button that stays pressed: bold on or off, following or not, a filter
applied or not. It looks like a [Button](?path=/docs/components-buttons-button--docs).

<Status of={ToggleButtonStories} />

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Default} />

## Variants

Unpressed is always the same neutral button, so the pressed one is the one
that stands out. `variant` and `appearance` choose how it looks when
pressed. Each pair below: unpressed, then pressed.

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Matrix} />

| Appearance when pressed | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `contained` | A toggle that should read as clearly on from across the screen: a filter, Follow. |
| `outlined` | A toggle among other outlined controls. Pressed, it fills neutral and keeps the variant's border. |
| `ghost` | Toolbars and dense rows: Bold, Italic, a star. Usually `isIconOnly`. |

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.IconOnly} />

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.WithIcon} />

From npm, or copied into your project through the registry:

```js
import { ToggleButton } from 'zweihander/toggle-button'
```

npx shadcn@latest add https://ontheshore.biz/zweihander/r/toggle-button.json

- Behaviour: [Base UI Toggle](https://base-ui.com/react/components/toggle)

`isLoading` a spinner takes the content's place.

for tables and dense rows, with a 14/20 label at both.

Unpressed is the same in every variant. Pressed and `contained` takes the
variant's solid, as on Button. Pressed `outlined` and `ghost` fill with the
neutral secondary instead of a tint of the variant: a toggle stays pressed
indefinitely, so its label has to pass 4.5:1 on the fill, and red text on a

## States

<States
  states={[
    { label: 'Unpressed' },
    { label: 'Pressed', content: <ToggleButton defaultPressed>Subscribe</ToggleButton> },
    { label: 'Hover', pseudo: 'hover' },
    { label: 'Focus', pseudo: 'focus-visible' },
    { label: 'Disabled', content: <Story of={ToggleButtonStories.Disabled} /> },
    { label: 'Loading', content: <Story of={ToggleButtonStories.Loading} /> },
  ]}
>
  <Story of={ToggleButtonStories.Default} />

Hover, focus, disabled and loading behave as on Button, in both the
pressed and the unpressed look. A toggle has no press-and-hold state:
holding the pointer down shows hover until it flips.

## API

{/* Storybook's table does not scroll by itself on a phone. */}
<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>
  <ArgTypes of={ToggleButtonStories} />
</div>

Every other `<button>` attribute passes through, including `ref`.

### Differences from the spec

- **Two sizes, not four.** The sizes follow Atlassian Design: 32px (`md`) by default, 24px (`sm`) for tables and dense rows. Both take 12px from the outer edge to the label (11px on ghost), a 6px gap and a 14/20 label; `sm` is a shorter box, not smaller type. The spec's larger steps were dropped; a big call to action is `md` with more room around it, not a taller box.
- **`pressed`, `defaultPressed`, `onPressedChange`** instead of
  `isSelected`: Base UI's names, per the kit's convention for components
  built on it. "Pressed" is also the ARIA word (`aria-pressed`).
- **`disabled`**, not `isDisabled`.
- **`variant` and `appearance` describe the pressed state.** The spec
  applies them to the button without saying what changes when it is
  selected. If unpressed also took them, a contained toggle would look
  pressed whether it was or not.
- **A pressed outlined or ghost toggle is filled neutral, not tinted with
  its variant.** It stays in that state indefinitely, so its label has to
  pass 4.5:1 on the fill.
- **`isIconOnly`**, as on Button.

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="guidelines">

## When to use

Use a toggle for a setting that is on or off and applies immediately:
Bold, Follow, a filter. The label names the setting, and stays the same in
both states.

<DoDont
  do={<Story of={ToggleButtonStories.DoSameLabel} />}
  doCaption="The label names the setting; pressed says it is on. A screen reader hears “Follow, toggle button, pressed”."
  dont={<Story of={ToggleButtonStories.DontSwitchLabel} />}
  dontCaption="A label that flips to the action reads as “Unfollow, pressed”, which contradicts itself."
/>

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Controlled} />

## When not to use

- **For a choice submitted with a form.** Use a Checkbox or a Switch: a
  toggle applies at once, a form field waits for Submit.
- **For one of many.** Put the toggles in a
  [Button Group](?path=/docs/components-buttons-buttongroup--docs), or use
  radios or Tabs. A lone toggle is independent: pressing one does not
  release another.
- **For an action.** Something that happens once (Save, Send) is a
  [Button](?path=/docs/components-buttons-button--docs).

## Accessibility

- A native `<button>` with `aria-pressed`, so a screen reader announces
  "Subscribe, toggle button, pressed".
- **Keep the label the same in both states.** `aria-pressed` carries the
  state; a label that switches from "Follow" to "Unfollow" as well reads
  as "Unfollow, pressed", which contradicts itself.
- Enter and Space both toggle it.
- `isIconOnly` needs `aria-label`, as on Button.
- `isLoading` keeps it focusable but inert, as on Button.
- 44×44px touch target at `sm` and `md`, from Button.

</DocTab>
</DocTabs>

'use client'

import { useId, useState, type ReactElement, type ReactNode } from 'react'
import { Tooltip as BaseTooltip } from '@base-ui/react/tooltip'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import styles from './Tooltip.module.css'

export interface TooltipProps {
  /** What the tooltip says. Short: a label or a hint, never the only way to learn something essential. */
  content: ReactNode
  /** The trigger: one focusable element, such as a Button. Its props are merged, not wrapped. */
  children: ReactElement
  side?: 'top' | 'right' | 'bottom' | 'left'
  align?: 'start' | 'center' | 'end'
  /** Milliseconds of hover before it opens. Focus opens it at once. */
  delay?: number
  closeDelay?: number
  open?: boolean
  defaultOpen?: boolean
  onOpenChange?: (open: boolean) => void
  /** Never open, e.g. while the trigger's label is already visible. */
  disabled?: boolean
  /** Where the tooltip renders instead of `<body>`, e.g. an element in fullscreen. */
  container?: HTMLElement | null
  className?: string
}

export function Tooltip({
  content,
  children,
  side = 'top',
  align = 'center',
  delay = 300,
  closeDelay = 0,
  open: openProp,
  defaultOpen = false,
  onOpenChange,
  disabled = false,
  container,
  className,
}: TooltipProps) {
  const id = useId()
  const [openState, setOpenState] = useState(defaultOpen)
  const open = openProp ?? openState
  return (
    <BaseTooltip.Root
      open={open}
      onOpenChange={(next) => {
        setOpenState(next)
        onOpenChange?.(next)
      }}
      disabled={disabled}
    >
      <BaseTooltip.Trigger
        delay={delay}
        closeDelay={closeDelay}
        render={children}
        // Base UI leaves tooltips out of the accessibility tree; while one is
        // open, point the trigger at it so it is read as a description.
        aria-describedby={open ? id : undefined}
      />
      <BaseTooltip.Portal container={container}>
        <BaseTooltip.Positioner className={styles.positioner} side={side} align={align} sideOffset={6}>
          <BaseTooltip.Popup id={id} role="tooltip" className={cn(styles.popup, className)}>
            {content}
          </BaseTooltip.Popup>
        </BaseTooltip.Positioner>
      </BaseTooltip.Portal>
    </BaseTooltip.Root>
  )
}

/** Tooltips inside share one delay: once one has opened, moving to the next opens it at once. */
export const TooltipGroup = BaseTooltip.Provider

# Tooltip A short label that appears when you hover over or focus a control: the name of a...
import { Meta, Canvas, Story, ArgTypes } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import { Anatomy, DocTab, DocTabs, DoDont, SpecTable, States, Status } from '../../../.storybook/blocks'
import * as TooltipStories from './Tooltip.stories'

<Meta of={TooltipStories} />

# Tooltip

<DocTabs>
<DocTab value="overview">

A short label that appears when you hover over or focus a control: the
name of an icon-only button, a keyboard shortcut, a one-line hint.

<Status of={TooltipStories} />

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.LongContent} />

## Variants

| Variant | When to use |
|---|---|
| Tooltip | A label or a one-line hint on a control. |

The tooltip opens on hover after a short delay and on keyboard focus at
once. Wrap a row of tooltips in `TooltipGroup` so that
once one has opened, moving to the next opens it without the delay:

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.Group} />

Only one tooltip is open at a time: opening one closes any other. Hover or
focus the triggers above to see them.

## Resources

From npm, or copied into your project through the registry:

```js
import { Tooltip, TooltipGroup } from 'zweihander/tooltip'
```

```sh
npx shadcn@latest add https://ontheshore.biz/zweihander/r/tooltip.json
```

- Source: [src/components/overlays/Tooltip.tsx](https://github.com/nguucode/zweihander/blob/main/src/components/overlays/Tooltip.tsx)
- Spec: [uiguideline.com/components/tooltip](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/tooltip)
- Behaviour: [Base UI Tooltip](https://base-ui.com/react/components/tooltip)
- Figma: not in the library yet

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="specs">

## Anatomy

<Anatomy parts={TooltipStories.anatomyParts}>
  <Story of={TooltipStories.Anatomy} />
</Anatomy>

The open tooltips on this tab and the next are pictures: real tooltips
held open and rendered in place with `container`, laid out above the
trigger where they open.

## Measurements

<SpecTable
  caption="Container"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Block padding', token: '--space-1' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Inline padding', token: '--space-1-5' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Corner radius', token: '--radius-sm' },
    { part: 'Text', property: 'Font size', token: '--text-body-sm' },
    { part: 'Text', property: 'Line height', token: '--leading-body-sm' },
  ]}
/>

The container is as wide as its text, at most 240px (15rem) and never wider than
the room beside the trigger; longer text wraps. It opens 6px from the
trigger, on the `--layer-tooltip` layer, above popovers and modals, so a
tooltip on a control inside one still shows. It fades in over
`--duration-fast`.

## Color

<SpecTable
  caption="Every tooltip"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Background', token: '--color-text' },
    { part: 'Text', property: 'Colour', token: '--color-surface' },
  ]}
/>

The tooltip is inverted in both modes: a tooltip is not part of the page, and the
dark-on-light (light-on-dark in dark mode) box says so, at the same
contrast as body text.

## States

<States
  states={[
    { label: 'Closed', content: <Story of={TooltipStories.Closed} /> },
    { label: 'Open', content: <Story of={TooltipStories.OpenPicture} /> },
  ]}
/>

- **Closed** until the pointer rests on the trigger for `delay` (300ms), or
  the trigger takes keyboard focus, which opens it at once.
- **Open** until Escape, blur or the pointer leaves, after `closeDelay`.
  Opening fades it in and scales it up from 96%.
- The trigger keeps the states of its own component; the tooltip has none
  of its own.
## API

{/* Storybook's table does not scroll by itself on a phone. */}
<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>
  <ArgTypes of={TooltipStories} />
</div>

`TooltipGroup` is Base UI's `Tooltip.Provider`: tooltips inside it share
one delay.

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="guidelines">

## When to use

Use a Tooltip for a label or a hint: the name of an icon-only button, a
keyboard shortcut, one line on what a control does. 300ms before it opens
is quick enough to feel responsive and long enough that tooltips do not
flash as the pointer crosses a toolbar.

<DoDont
  do={<Story of={TooltipStories.DoShortLabel} />}
  doCaption="A short label that repeats the icon-only button's name for sighted users."
  dont={<Story of={TooltipStories.DontEssentialInfo} />}
  dontCaption="Rules the reader needs to fill the field. Touch cannot open a tooltip, and it hides as soon as focus moves on: put the rules under the field."
/>

It opens on the `side` given, top by default. When that side has no room,
it flips to the other one.

## When not to use

- **For anything a reader needs to finish a task.** Put it on the page: a
  tooltip cannot be reached by touch, and it disappears the moment you
  look away.
- **For links, buttons or other interactive content.** Hover and touch
  cannot reach the tooltip. Use a
  [Popover](?path=/docs/components-overlays-popover--docs).
- **For a rich preview.** A tooltip holds text only. Use a
  [Popover](?path=/docs/components-overlays-popover--docs) with
  `openOnHover`.
- **On a disabled button.** It is not focusable, so its tooltip never opens
  by keyboard. Put the reason it is disabled in text next to it.

## Accessibility

- It opens on hover after `delay` and on keyboard focus at once, and
  closes on Escape, blur or pointer leave.

  <Canvas of={TooltipStories.Default} />

- Base UI keeps tooltips out of the accessibility tree. This component
  gives the popup `role="tooltip"` and, while it is open, points the
  trigger's `aria-describedby` at it, so it is read as a description.
- It is a **description, not a name.** An icon-only button still needs its
  own `aria-label`; the tooltip then shows that label to sighted users too.
- The trigger must be focusable: a Button, a link, a field.
- `--color-surface` on `--color-text` reads at 16:1 or more in both modes.

</DocTab>
</DocTabs>

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import docs from './docs.module.css'

const BREAKPOINTS = [
  { name: 'base', min: '0', px: '0px' },
  { name: 'sm', min: '40rem', px: '640px' },
  { name: 'md', min: '48rem', px: '768px' },
  { name: 'lg', min: '64rem', px: '1024px' },
  { name: 'xl', min: '80rem', px: '1280px' },
  { name: '2xl', min: '96rem', px: '1536px' },
] as const

// One row per breakpoint; each hides itself once the next one is reached, so
// exactly one is visible and it is the active one. Resize the preview to see
// it change.
const ACTIVE = [
  docs.bpBase,
  docs.bpSm,
  docs.bpMd,
  docs.bpLg,
  docs.bpXl,
  docs.bp2xl,
] as const

function ActiveBreakpoint() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {BREAKPOINTS.map((bp, i) => (
        <div key={bp.name} className={`${ACTIVE[i]} ${docs.bpChip}`}>
          <span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-mono)', fontSize: 'var(--text-body)', fontWeight: 500 }}>
            {bp.name}
          </span>
          <span style={{ fontSize: 'var(--text-body-sm)', opacity: 0.8 }}>
            active from {bp.min} ({bp.px}) up
          </span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

function Ladder() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {BREAKPOINTS.filter((b) => b.name !== 'base').map((bp) => (
        <div key={bp.name} className={docs.row} style={{ gap: 'var(--space-3)' }}>
          <span className={docs.caption} style={{ width: '2.5rem', flexShrink: 0 }}>{bp.name}</span>
          <div
            style={{
              height: '1rem',
              borderRadius: 'var(--radius-sm)',
              background: 'var(--color-background-neutral)',
              width: `calc(${bp.min} / 96 * 100%)`,
            }}
          />
          <span className={docs.caption}>{bp.px}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

# Breakpoints Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without modifi...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as BreakpointsStories from './Breakpoints.stories'

<Meta of={BreakpointsStories} />

# Breakpoints

Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without
modification. Zweihänder declares no `--breakpoint-*` of its own.

| Prefix | Min width | At a 16px root |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(none)* | `0` | 0px |
| `sm:` | `40rem` | 640px |
| `md:` | `48rem` | 768px |
| `lg:` | `64rem` | 1024px |
| `xl:` | `80rem` | 1280px |
| `2xl:` | `96rem` | 1536px |

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Scale} />

The box below reports the breakpoint currently in effect. Resize the
preview — or use Storybook's viewport toolbar — and it changes.

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Active} />

## They are min-width, and that has a direction

`md:flex` means "flex at 768px **and above**". There is no maximum, so
rules outside a media query are the small-screen case and every
`@media (width >= …)` is an override for larger screens. Write the phone
layout first and widen it; writing the desktop layout first means every
breakpoint has to undo something.

The other direction is expressible — `@media (width < 48rem)` caps a rule
below a breakpoint — but mixing both in one component is where responsive
CSS usually becomes unreadable. Pick min-width and stay there.

## Breakpoints are in rem

`40rem`, not `640px`. A reader who raises their browser's default font
size gets the layout to break earlier, because the layout responds to how
large the text actually is rather than to the device. That is the correct
behaviour and it is worth not overriding: a `px` breakpoint holds a
multi-column layout together long after its text has stopped fitting.

The px column above is only true at the default 16px root.

## The kit has no opinion yet

**No component here uses a breakpoint.** Controls such as Button and Text
Input are inline-sized — they fill whatever their container gives them and have no
layout of their own to rearrange. The stories on this page are the only
responsive code in the repo.

That is expected: breakpoints are a **layout** concern, and the kit ships
components, not page layouts. Marketing sections, dashboards and checkout
flows are where these will actually get used, and where the kit will need an opinion about
which of the five are load-bearing. Most design systems end up leaning on
two or three.

## Container queries are usually the better tool

A breakpoint asks how wide the *viewport* is. A component almost always
wants to know how wide **its own container** is — the same card is narrow
in a sidebar and wide in a main column at one identical viewport width.

Container queries are in every current browser, and they are plain CSS:

```css
.card {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.cardBody {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

@container (width >= 28rem) {
  .cardBody {
    flex-direction: row;
  }
}
```

When a component is built here that needs to reflow, it should reach for
`@container` first and a viewport breakpoint only when the thing being
arranged really is the page.

## Customization

Breakpoints are theme keys like any other, redefined in the `@theme`
block:

```css
@theme {
  --breakpoint-sm: 30rem;
  --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem;
}
```

Two cautions. These generate utility *variants*, so they cannot be
overridden per-scope by `Theme` the way a color can — a variant is
compiled into a media query at build time, and there is no runtime
variable to swap. And removing a default breakpoint removes its prefix
entirely, so any existing `lg:` becomes a silent no-op rather than an
error.

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import docs from './docs.module.css'
import { PALETTE, STEPS } from './palette'

function BandSwatches({ pairs }: { pairs: readonly (readonly [string, string])[] }) {
  return (
    <div className={docs.grid}>
      {pairs.map(([bg, fg]) => (
        <div
          key={bg}
          className={docs.swatchPair}
          style={{ background: `var(--${bg})`, color: `var(--${fg})` }}
        >
          <span className={docs.swatchLabel}>--{bg}</span>
          <span className={docs.swatchLabel}>--{fg}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

const LINES = ['color-border', 'color-border-input', 'color-border-bold', 'color-border-focused'] as const

function LineSwatches() {
  return (
    <div style={{ display: 'flex', gap: 'var(--space-6)' }}>
      {LINES.map((token) => (
        <div
          key={token}
          style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', alignItems: 'center', gap: 'var(--space-2)' }}
        >
          <div
            style={{
              height: '2.5rem',
              width: '6rem',
              borderRadius: 'var(--radius-md)',
              boxShadow: `inset 0 0 0 2px var(--${token})`,
            }}
          />
          <span className={docs.caption}>--{token}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

function PrimitiveSwatches() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {Object.entries(PALETTE).map(([hue, values]) => (
        <div key={hue} className={docs.rampRow}>
          <span className={docs.rampName}>{hue}</span>
          <div className={docs.ramp}>
            {values.map((value, i) => (
              <div
                key={STEPS[i]}
                title={`${hue}-${STEPS[i]}`}
                className={docs.rampStep}
                style={{ background: value }}
              />
            ))}
          </div>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

# Colors Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in `src/tokens.css`, ...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ColorsStories from './Colors.stories'

<Meta of={ColorsStories} />

# Colors

Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in
`src/tokens.css`, with a counterpart under the `.dark` class. The source is
`tokens/semantic.json`; `npm run tokens` generates the stylesheet from it
and measures the contrast pairs listed below. One stylesheet holds both
modes, so a rule that reads `var(--color-text)` switches theme without a
conditional.

**The swatches on this page read their values out of the live document**,
so a color shown here is the value the components get. The token *names*
are listed by hand in `Colors.stories.tsx`.

## Naming

Names follow Atlassian's design tokens:

```
--color-<category>-<role>[-<emphasis>]
```

The **category** says what the color is painted on: `surface`, `text`,
`icon`, `border`, `background`, `interaction`, `blanket` or `chart`. Pick
the category by the CSS property you are setting — a `color` on a label is
a `text` token, a `fill` on a glyph is an `icon` token, a `background` on a
button is a `background` token. The bare category (`--color-text`,
`--color-border`) is the default for it.

The **role** says what it means: `brand`, `neutral`, `input`, `selected`,
a status (`info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`), or `accent-<hue>`.

The **emphasis** says how strong it is, from weakest to strongest:
`subtlest`, `subtle`, (none), `bold`, `bolder`. `-inverse` is text or an
icon that sits on a `bold` fill of the same role.

In Figma the Color collection mirrors this as `<category>/<role>`:
`text/subtlest`, `background/brand-bold`, and `text/default` for the bare
`--color-text`. Each variable's code syntax is its `var(--color-…)`, so
Dev Mode shows the CSS name.

## Surfaces

What a region of the page is. `--color-surface` is the page;
`--color-surface-raised` is a card or panel set into it;
`--color-surface-overlay` is anything that floats above it — a menu,
popover, modal or toast. In light mode the page is gray-50 and the two
raised surfaces are white, so a panel separates by being lighter and needs
a border at most. In dark mode the page is the darkest step and both
raised surfaces are lifted one step toward the viewer.

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-surface` | The page | gray-50 | gray-950 |
| `--color-surface-raised` | A card or panel in the page | white | gray-900 |
| `--color-surface-overlay` | A menu, popover, modal or toast | white | gray-900 |

Text on any surface is `--color-text` (or a quieter text token below).
There is no per-surface foreground: one text token works on all three.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Surfaces} />

## Text

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-text` | Body text, headings, labels | gray-950 | gray-50 |
| `--color-text-subtle` | Text that recedes until hovered or current: navigation labels | gray-600 | gray-300 |
| `--color-text-subtlest` | Secondary text: descriptions, hints, captions, placeholders | gray-500 | gray-400 |
| `--color-text-inverse` | Text on `--color-background-neutral-bold` | gray-50 | gray-50 |
| `--color-text-brand` | Brand-coloured text: an outlined or ghost primary button, a link | accent text step | accent text step |
| `--color-text-brand-bold` | Text on `--color-background-brand-subtlest` | accent-800 or darker | accent-300 or lighter |
| `--color-text-brand-inverse` | Label on `--color-background-brand-bold` | white or near-black, per accent | near-black |
| `--color-text-<status>` | Status text on the page or on its tint | 800 | 300 |
| `--color-text-<status>-inverse` | Label on `--color-background-<status>-bold` | neutral-50 (warning: neutral-900) | neutral-900 |
| `--color-text-accent-<hue>` | Hue text on the page or on its tint | 800 | 300 |
| `--color-text-accent-<hue>-inverse` | Label on `--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder` | neutral-50 | neutral-50 |

`--color-text-subtle` is body-safe (7.24:1 on the light page). Use
`--color-text-subtlest` for genuinely secondary text; it still clears 4.5:1
on every surface and fill it is allowed on (see Contrast).

`--color-text-brand` is a separate step from the brand fill. The fill is
picked so its label reads; read as text on the page, amber-500 is barely
2:1, so the build picks the first step of the accent that clears 4.5:1
against the page instead.

## Icons

Glyphs take `icon` tokens, not `text` tokens. They are separate so an icon
can sit at a different step from the text beside it: a status icon is the
saturated hue, its text the darker 800 step.

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-icon` | Default glyph | gray-950 | gray-50 |
| `--color-icon-subtle` | A glyph that recedes: a chevron, a field's leading icon | gray-500 | gray-400 |
| `--color-icon-inverse` | A glyph on a bold neutral fill | gray-50 | gray-50 |
| `--color-icon-brand` | A brand-coloured glyph | accent text step | accent text step |
| `--color-icon-info` | Info glyph | blue-600 | blue-400 |
| `--color-icon-success` | Success glyph | green-700 | green-400 |
| `--color-icon-warning` | Warning glyph | amber-600 | amber-400 |
| `--color-icon-danger` | Danger glyph | red-600 | red-400 |

## Borders

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-border` | A divider or container edge | gray-200 | white 10% |
| `--color-border-input` | A text field's edge | gray-300 | white 18% |
| `--color-border-bold` | A checkbox, radio or switch track outline | gray-500 | gray-400 |
| `--color-border-focused` | The focus indicator | accent-700 | accent-400 |

Choose by what the edge has to do. `--color-border` separates things and
is never the only sign something is there. `--color-border-input` is the
light hairline of a text field: about 1.5:1, a deliberate exception to 3:1
because a field also has its label, placeholder, fill and focus ring. A
product that needs 3:1 on fields sets
`--color-border-input: var(--color-border-bold)`. `--color-border-bold` is
for controls that have nothing else showing they are there, so it clears
3:1 against the page (WCAG 1.4.11). `--color-border-focused` follows the
accent one step darker than its fill, because the lighter solids miss 3:1
against the page — yellow-600 measures 2.93:1.

In dark mode the two lighter borders are translucent white, so an edge
reads the same on `--color-surface` and on a lifted
`--color-surface-raised`.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.LinesAndFocus} />

## Backgrounds

Fills behind content that is not a surface: a button, a selected row, a
filled field, a status message.

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-background-neutral` | A quiet fill: secondary button, a disabled field, a zebra stripe | gray-100 | gray-800 |
| `--color-background-neutral-bold` | A solid neutral fill (a neutral Avatar) | gray-600 | gray-600 |
| `--color-background-selected` | The current item: a selected row, the active nav item | gray-200 | white 10% |
| `--color-background-input` | A filled panel or field that subtlest text can sit on | gray-50 | gray-800 |
| `--color-background-brand-bold` | The default button: **the brand hue** | accent solid | accent solid |
| `--color-background-brand-subtlest` | A brand tint | accent-100 | accent-950 |
| `--color-background-<status>-bold` | Solid status fill | 600 (success 700, warning 500) | 400 |
| `--color-background-<status>` | Status tint | 100 | 950 |
| `--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder` | Solid hue fill (a solid Tag) | 600 | 600 |
| `--color-background-accent-<hue>-subtler` | Hue tint | 100 | 950 |

`--color-background-brand-bold` is the one fill the
[`accentColor`](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) setting moves, with
`--color-text-brand`, `--color-icon-brand`, the brand tint and
`--color-border-focused`. The accent solid is step 600 for most hues and
700 for sky, fuchsia, pink and rose in light mode, and its label is white
or near-black, whichever clears 4.5:1 on it.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SubtleSurfaces} />

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SolidActions} />

## Interaction, blanket

| Token | Role | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-interaction-hovered` | Hover overlay, laid over whatever fill the item already has | black 5% | white 6% |
| `--color-blanket` | Behind a modal | black 50% | black 50% |

`--color-interaction-hovered` is translucent so one token works on any
surface or fill: lay it on top (a second background layer or a
pseudo-element), do not swap the fill for it.

## Status and hue

Four status roles carry meaning about state: `info` (blue), `success`
(green), `warning` (amber), `danger` (red). They are fixed hues and do not
follow the accent: a status colour that changes with the brand stops being
a status. Each role has a solid fill and its label, a tint, text that reads
on the tint or the page, and an icon:

```
--color-background-<status>-bold   --color-text-<status>-inverse
--color-background-<status>        --color-text-<status>
--color-icon-<status>
```

`danger` is also the destructive action: a delete button is
`--color-background-danger-bold` with `--color-text-danger-inverse`. If the
accent is already red, tell a destructive action apart by wording and
placement, not by colour alone.

The 17 hues (`red` to `rose`, as in the primitives below) carry category,
not state — a Tag colour, an Avatar's initials. Each has a solid, its
label, a tint, and text:

```
--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder   --color-text-accent-<hue>-inverse
--color-background-accent-<hue>-subtler  --color-text-accent-<hue>
```

Every hue's solid is step 600 with a white label in both modes, so a row of
solid tags reads as one set. The warm hues fall below 4.5:1 there, and the
build does not measure hue labels on purpose (decision of 2026-10-08).
`--color-text-accent-orange-contrast` is a near-black label (neutral-900)
for orange, for a place that has to pass 4.5:1 on the orange solid; nothing
in the kit reads it yet.

## Chart

`--color-chart-1` to `--color-chart-8` colour series in the charts, in
order. They are separate from the hue tokens so the series order can be
tuned for neighbours that stay distinguishable.

| Token | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-chart-1` | blue-600 | blue-400 |
| `--color-chart-2` | yellow-700 | yellow-400 |
| `--color-chart-3` | pink-600 | pink-400 |
| `--color-chart-4` | teal-600 | teal-500 |
| `--color-chart-5` | violet-600 | violet-400 |
| `--color-chart-6` | orange-600 | orange-500 |
| `--color-chart-7` | cyan-600 | cyan-500 |
| `--color-chart-8` | lime-700 | lime-500 |

## Contrast

Measured, not assumed. `npm run tokens` computes each pair below from the
OKLCH values and stops the build if one drops under its floor. WCAG AA
wants 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for the edge of a control or a chart mark.

- **Brand labels:** for each of the 17 accents, the solid and its label are
  picked together so `--color-text-brand-inverse` clears 4.5:1 on
  `--color-background-brand-bold`. `--color-text-brand` clears 4.5:1
  against the page, and `--color-border-focused` clears 3:1 against it.
- **Status:** for each of info, success, warning and danger, in both modes,
  `--color-text-<status>-inverse` on the bold fill, and
  `--color-text-<status>` on its tint and on the page, all at 4.5:1.
- **Hues:** `--color-text-accent-<hue>` on its subtler tint and on the
  page, at 4.5:1. Labels on the bolder fill are not measured (see above).
- **Secondary text:** `--color-text-subtlest` on `--color-surface`,
  `--color-surface-raised`, `--color-background-input` and
  `--color-background-neutral`, at 4.5:1 on all nine gray ramps in both
  modes.
- **Neutral solid:** `--color-text-inverse` on
  `--color-background-neutral-bold`, at 4.5:1 on all nine gray ramps.
- **Control outlines:** `--color-border-bold` against the page, at 3:1 on
  all nine gray ramps.
- **Chart marks:** each `--color-chart-<n>` against `--color-surface-raised`,
  at 3:1 on all nine gray ramps. This is why yellow and lime take step 700
  in light.

The values on the defaults (blue accent, gray ramp):

| Pair | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-text` on `--color-surface` | 19.28:1 | 19.28:1 |
| `--color-text` on `--color-surface-raised` | 20.13:1 | 17.00:1 |
| `--color-text-subtle` on `--color-surface` | 7.24:1 | 13.67:1 |
| `--color-text-subtlest` on `--color-surface` | 4.85:1 | 7.73:1 |
| `--color-text-subtlest` on `--color-background-neutral` | 4.60:1 | 5.64:1 |
| `--color-text-brand-inverse` on `--color-background-brand-bold` | 5.03:1 | 6.79:1 |
| `--color-text-brand` on `--color-surface` | 5.04:1 | 7.63:1 |
| `--color-text-inverse` on `--color-background-neutral-bold` | 7.24:1 | 7.24:1 |
| `--color-border-focused` on `--color-surface` | 6.54:1 | 7.63:1 |
| `--color-border-bold` on `--color-surface` | 4.85:1 | 7.73:1 |

| Status pair | info | success | warning | danger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| label on bold, light | 5.03:1 | 4.73:1 | 8.35:1 | 4.56:1 |
| text on tint, light | 7.25:1 | 6.45:1 | 6.41:1 | 6.86:1 |
| text on page, light | 8.47:1 | 6.80:1 | 6.83:1 | 8.02:1 |
| label on bold, dark | 6.79:1 | 10.09:1 | 10.43:1 | 6.19:1 |
| text on tint, dark | 8.13:1 | 10.67:1 | 10.37:1 | 8.40:1 |
| text on page, dark | 11.11:1 | 14.40:1 | 13.92:1 | 10.48:1 |

The tightest pair is `--color-text-subtlest` on
`--color-background-neutral` in light mode, at 4.60:1: gray-500 on every
ramp is the lightest value that clears 4.6:1 on its own gray-100. Dark
`--color-text-danger-inverse` is neutral-900, not near-white: the danger
fill lightens to red-400 in dark mode, and near-white on red-400 is 2.77:1.

## Color is never the only signal

`--color-background-danger-bold` on a button does not say what will be
destroyed, and a red tag means nothing to a reader who cannot tell it from
a neutral one. Pair colour with words, an icon or a shape every time it
carries meaning. The numbers above are a floor, not a design review.

## Dark mode

Every token has a counterpart under `.dark`, switched by a class. Dark is
not an inversion of light: surfaces go *up*, and strong fills get lighter
so their labels flip to dark text. The mechanism and how to follow the OS
setting are on their own page:
**[Dark mode](?path=/docs/foundations-dark-mode--docs)**.

## Primitives

The palette underneath: 17 hues and 9 gray ramps, 11 shades each. Two ramps feed the semantic
tokens and each can be swapped on its own: an **accent** (blue by default)
for the brand tokens, and a **gray** (`gray` by default) for surfaces,
text, borders and neutral fills. The status, hue and chart tokens pin
their own ramps. The exceptions to "every value is a ramp step" are the
white raised surfaces in light mode and the translucent tokens: the dark
borders, dark selected fill, hover overlay and blanket.

This is raw material, not a palette to build UI from. Reach for a
primitive when you are defining the *next* semantic token; if a primitive
shows up in a component, a token is missing. The classes are generated by
an `@source inline(...)` directive in `src/index.css` only so this page
can render them.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Primitives} />

## Migrating from 0.8

0.9.0 renamed every colour token and removed the old names. The main ones:

{/* docs:check allow --background --card --popover --foreground --card-foreground --popover-foreground --secondary-foreground --accent-foreground --muted-foreground --subtle-foreground --primary --primary-foreground --primary-text --secondary --muted --accent --selected --surface-filled --border --input --field-border --control-border --ring --destructive --destructive-foreground --neutral-solid --neutral-solid-foreground --hover-overlay --scrim --warning-indicator -- old 0.8 names, listed for migration */}

| 0.8 | 0.9 |
| --- | --- |
| `--background` | `--color-surface` |
| `--card` | `--color-surface-raised` |
| `--popover` | `--color-surface-overlay` |
| `--foreground`, `--card-foreground`, `--popover-foreground`, `--secondary-foreground`, `--accent-foreground` | `--color-text` |
| `--subtle-foreground` | `--color-text-subtle` |
| `--muted-foreground` | `--color-text-subtlest` |
| `--primary` | `--color-background-brand-bold` |
| `--primary-foreground` | `--color-text-brand-inverse` |
| `--primary-text` | `--color-text-brand` |
| `--secondary`, `--muted`, `--accent` | `--color-background-neutral` |
| `--selected` | `--color-background-selected` |
| `--surface-filled` | `--color-background-input` |
| `--neutral-solid`, `--neutral-solid-foreground` | `--color-background-neutral-bold`, `--color-text-inverse` |
| `--border`, `--input` | `--color-border` |
| `--field-border` | `--color-border-input` |
| `--control-border` | `--color-border-bold` |
| `--ring` | `--color-border-focused` |
| `--destructive`, `--destructive-foreground` | `--color-background-danger-bold`, `--color-text-danger-inverse` |
| `--hover-overlay` | `--color-interaction-hovered` |
| `--scrim` | `--color-blanket` |
| `--warning-indicator` | `--color-icon-warning` |
| --&lt;status&gt;, --&lt;status&gt;-foreground | `--color-background-<status>-bold`, `--color-text-<status>-inverse` |
| --&lt;status&gt;-subtle, --&lt;status&gt;-text | `--color-background-<status>`, `--color-text-<status>` |
| --&lt;hue&gt;, --&lt;hue&gt;-foreground | `--color-background-accent-<hue>-bolder`, `--color-text-accent-<hue>-inverse` |
| --&lt;hue&gt;-subtle, --&lt;hue&gt;-text | `--color-background-accent-<hue>-subtler`, `--color-text-accent-<hue>` |
| --chart-N | `--color-chart-<n>` |

Glyphs that used a text token now have their own: `--color-icon`,
`--color-icon-subtle` and the status icons.

## Customization

Redeclare a token after Zweihänder's stylesheet, or edit
`tokens/semantic.json` and run `npm run tokens` if you own the source.
Nothing that reads `var(--color-background-brand-bold)` changes, because
every rule points at the variable rather than the value.

Two things to carry through a rebrand: re-measure the pairs above — a
brand hue at the same lightness as another will not hit the same ratios —
and keep light and dark as separate decisions. Reusing the light value of
a fill in dark mode is what produced the 2.77:1 failure described under
Contrast.

Projects that install through the registry get these values merged into
their own stylesheet; projects on the npm package import
`zweihander/tokens.css` and override afterwards.

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import { expect } from 'storybook/test'
import { Button } from '@/components/buttons/Button'
import { TextInput } from '@/components/inputs/TextInput'
import docs from './docs.module.css'

const TOKENS = [
  {
    token: '--cursor-button',
    value: 'default',
    usage: 'Button, and anything that acts on the current page',
    note: "Matches the browser's own convention: an interactive element that doesn't navigate keeps the regular arrow, not a hand.",
    demo: <Button>Button</Button>,
  },
  {
    token: '--cursor-link',
    value: 'pointer',
    usage: 'A Button rendered as a real link',
    note: 'A Button with href renders a real <a href>, which navigates — so it keeps the hand the browser gives every other link.',
    demo: <Button href="#cursors">Link</Button>,
  },
  {
    token: '--cursor-disabled',
    value: 'not-allowed',
    usage: 'A disabled control that stays hoverable',
    note: 'TextInput uses this. Button does not — its disabled state is pointer-events: none, so it is never hovered and a cursor there would be dead CSS.',
    demo: (
      <div style={{ width: '9rem' }}>
        <TextInput aria-label="Disabled" placeholder="Disabled" disabled isFullWidth />
      </div>
    ),
  },
] as const

function CursorTokens() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stackWide} style={{ gap: 'var(--space-4)' }}>
      {TOKENS.map(({ token, value, usage, note, demo }) => (
        <div
          key={token}
          className={docs.card}
          style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', gap: 'var(--space-2)' }}
        >
          <div style={{ display: 'flex', alignItems: 'center', gap: 'var(--space-4)' }}>
            {/* Real components rather than a styled div, so what you hover is
                what ships — a div with cursor set on it would demonstrate the
                token but not that any component actually reads it. */}
            <div style={{ width: '9rem', flexShrink: 0 }}>{demo}</div>
            <div style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column' }}>
              <span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-mono)', fontSize: 'var(--text-body)' }}>
                {token}
              </span>
              <span className={docs.caption}>{value}</span>
            </div>
          </div>
          <p className={docs.note}>
            <strong style={{ color: 'var(--color-text)', fontWeight: 500 }}>{usage}.</strong> {note}
          </p>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

# Cursors Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do not get ...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as CursorsStories from './Cursors.stories'

<Meta of={CursorsStories} />

# Cursors

Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do
not get `cursor: pointer`. Links do.**

## The convention

`cursor: pointer` means "this navigates" — it is the hand that appears
over a link. Browsers have never applied it to `<button>`, `<select>` or a
checkbox, and neither does this kit. Interactive elements that act on the
current page keep the regular arrow; only a link gets the hand. This is a
deliberate departure from the very common `button { cursor: pointer }`
reset.

It is worth knowing the argument on the other side: a large body of
usability opinion holds that the hand cursor is now such a widespread
affordance for "clickable" that removing it costs more than the semantic
purity gains. If your product takes that view, this is a one-line change —
see **Customization** below. The point of making it a token is that it is
one line, in one place, rather than a decision re-litigated per component.

<Canvas of={CursorsStories.Tokens} />

## `--cursor-button`

`default` — the regular arrow. Applied by Button.

Note this changes nothing visually today: a native `<button>` already
shows the arrow. **The token's job is not its current value; it is that
the value is reachable.** Without it, switching the kit to `pointer` means
editing every component; with it, it is one declaration.

## `--cursor-link`

`pointer` — the hand.

This one exists because the convention above has a second half that is
easy to state and easy to get wrong. Button takes `href`, so it can
render as a real `<a href>` — and when it did, it inherited
`--cursor-button` and lost the hand that the browser gives every other
link on the page. A link styled as a button is still a link.

```css
a[href].button {
  cursor: var(--cursor-link);
}
```

The `a[href]` part is doing real work. An `<a>` without `href` is not a
link and browsers do not give it the hand either, so matching on the
attribute rather than the element keeps the rule honest.

The distinction the kit draws is navigation versus action, not
appearance: a `<button>` styled as a link would still act on the current
page, so it would keep the arrow.

| | Element | Cursor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<Button>` | `<button>` | arrow |
| `<Button href="/x">` | `<a href>` | hand |

The Button `Href` story asserts this, and compares against a bare
`<a href>` rather than the literal `pointer` — so overriding
`--cursor-link` moves the assertion with it instead of breaking it.

## `--cursor-disabled`

`not-allowed` — used by TextInput, and **not** by Button. That asymmetry
is not an oversight.

A disabled `<input>` stays hit-testable, so a cursor set on it renders and
the user gets feedback on hover. Button's disabled state is
`pointer-events: none`, which makes the element untargetable; an
untargetable element is never hovered, so a cursor there would be dead
CSS. The `pointer-events: none` is not incidental — because Button
can render as an `<a>`, which ignores the `disabled` attribute entirely. Blocking pointer events is what actually disables it
in that case.

So the token applies to the pattern where a control stays hoverable while
disabled — including a control deliberately wrapped so a tooltip can
explain *why*. That trade-off, between a disabled control you can
interrogate and one that is inert, is a real design choice, and the two
components here happen to sit on opposite sides of it.

## Adding tokens

A mature system ends up with a token per interactive component —
checkboxes, menu items, radios, switches, slider thumbs. This kit has
three, because it has two components and one of them can render as two
different things.

{/* docs:check allow --cursor-slider-thumb -- an example of a token not to add */}

**Add a token when the component that needs it is built, not before.** A
`--cursor-slider-thumb` with no Slider is a value nobody can verify and
that the eventual Slider may not want.

## Customization

All three are plain CSS keywords, not colors, so they override like any
other custom property:

```css
:root {
  --cursor-button: pointer;
}
```

Load any override after Zweihänder's own stylesheet so the cascade picks it
up. Setting `--cursor-button: pointer` is the one-line version of adopting
the mainstream convention; it leaves `--cursor-link` alone, which is
already `pointer`, so the two simply converge.

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import { expect } from 'storybook/test'
import { Button } from '@/components/buttons/Button'
import { TextInput } from '@/components/inputs/TextInput'
import { Theme } from '@/theme/Theme'
import docs from './docs.module.css'

const PAIRS = [
  ['color-surface', 'color-text'],
  ['color-surface-raised', 'color-text'],
  ['color-background-brand-bold', 'color-text-brand-inverse'],
  ['color-background-neutral', 'color-text-subtlest'],
  ['color-background-danger-bold', 'color-text-danger-inverse'],
] as const

function Swatches() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {PAIRS.map(([bg, fg]) => (
        <div
          key={bg}
          style={{
            display: 'flex',
            alignItems: 'center',
            justifyContent: 'space-between',
            borderRadius: 'var(--radius-md)',
            border: '1px solid var(--color-border)',
            padding: 'var(--space-2) var(--space-3)',
            background: `var(--${bg})`,
            color: `var(--${fg})`,
          }}
        >
          <span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-mono)', fontSize: 'var(--text-body-sm)' }}>--{bg}</span>
          <span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-mono)', fontSize: 'var(--text-body-sm)', opacity: 0.7 }}>--{fg}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

function Sample() {
  return (
    <div style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', gap: 'var(--space-4)', background: 'var(--color-surface)', color: 'var(--color-text)', padding: 'var(--space-4)' }}>
      <Swatches />
      <TextInput label="Email" placeholder="you@example.com" />
      <div style={{ display: 'flex', gap: 'var(--space-2)' }}>
        <Button>Save</Button>
        <Button variant="destructive">Delete</Button>
        <Button variant="secondary" appearance="outlined">Cancel</Button>
      </div>
    </div>
  )
}

    await expect(getComputedStyle(light).colorScheme).toBe('light')

import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as DarkModeStories from './DarkMode.stories'

<Meta of={DarkModeStories} />

# Dark mode

Dark mode is **a class, not a media query.** `tokens.css` declares the
light values on `:root, .light` and the dark values on `.dark`, and
every rule in the kit reads those variables, so the class is the only
switch there is. The same scopes set `color-scheme`, so the UI the browser
draws itself (scrollbars, date and select popups, autofill) switches with
them.

Nothing is automatic about it. Adding `class="dark"` to `<html>` is what
switches the document; without that, a device set to dark mode gets the
light theme. That is the trade — see **Following the system** below.

<Canvas of={DarkModeStories.SideBySide} />

## Components don't know about it

No component stylesheet — `Button.module.css`, `InputField.module.css` or any other — mentions `.dark`.
They write `background: var(--color-background-brand-bold)`, and it is the variable that
changes; the rule is identical in both modes.

This is the main reason to reach for a token rather than a literal. A
hard-coded `#0a0a0a` is near-black in both modes and needs a `.dark`
override beside it to survive a theme switch; `var(--color-background-brand-bold)` needs
nothing. Every theme conditional in a codebase is a place a value was
hardcoded and then patched.

## Dark is not an inversion

Flipping lightness would produce the wrong result in three places, and the
palette deliberately doesn't:

- **`--color-surface` is gray-950, not black.** A pure-black page makes
  the halation around light text worse and leaves no room to sit a surface
  *below* the page level.
- **Surfaces go up, not down.** `--color-surface-raised` and
  `--color-surface-overlay` are a step *lighter* than the page in dark
  mode (gray-900 on gray-950), as they are in light mode (white on
  gray-50). Elevation in dark mode is carried by lightness, because a drop shadow
  has almost nothing left to darken (see
  [Shadows](?path=/docs/foundations-shadows--docs)).
- **Strong fills become light, so their labels become dark.**
  `--color-background-brand-bold` goes from the accent's 600 step to its
  400, and `--color-text-brand-inverse` turns near-black with it.
  `--color-background-danger-bold` does the same, red-600 to red-400 —
  which is exactly where the palette's one contrast bug lived: keeping the
  near-white `--color-text-danger-inverse` on the lightened red measured
  2.77:1. It is now neutral-900 at 6.19:1. Lightening a fill without
  flipping its `-inverse` label is the single easiest dark-mode mistake to
  make.

Full measurements for both modes are in
[Color → Contrast](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs).

## Alpha for edges

`--color-border` and `--color-border-input` are opaque gray-200 and
gray-300 in light, and `white / 10%` and `white / 18%` in dark;
`--color-background-selected` is `white / 10%` in dark too. An opaque dark
border would have to be re-chosen for every surface it sits on; a
translucent white edge lightens whatever is underneath, so the same token
reads correctly on `--color-surface` and on a lifted
`--color-surface-raised`. `--color-interaction-hovered` and
`--color-blanket` are translucent in both modes for the same reason.

## Scoping

`Theme` switches an appearance for a subtree rather than the document —
a dark footer on a light page, a light popover inside a dark shell. See
[Overview → Nesting](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) for how the
nesting resolves and the one caveat that comes with it.

```tsx
<Theme appearance="dark">
  <Footer />
</Theme>
```

## Following the system

The kit ships no `prefers-color-scheme` handling, because the choice
between "follow the OS" and "remember what the user picked" belongs to the
app, not the component library. The usual shape:

```ts
const media = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')
const stored = localStorage.getItem('theme') // 'light' | 'dark' | null
const dark = stored ? stored === 'dark' : media.matches
document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark', dark)
```

Two things worth getting right. Run it **before first paint** — in a
blocking inline script in `<head>`, not in a `useEffect` — or the page
renders light and flips, which is the flash every themed site has had at
some point. And keep listening to `media` afterwards so a user changing
their OS setting mid-session is followed, unless they have made an
explicit choice.

In this Storybook, the **Theme** toolbar control does the class toggle for
you; there is no persistence and no system detection.

const example = (
  <Button startIcon={<Icon name="plus" />} size="md">
    Add item

const tabs = (
  <DocTabs>
    <DocTab value="overview">
      <p>What it is.</p>
    </DocTab>
    <DocTab value="specs">
      <p>How it is built.</p>
    </DocTab>
    <DocTab value="guidelines">
      <p>How to use it.</p>
    </DocTab>
  </DocTabs>
)

export const Tabs: Story = {
  render: () => tabs,
  play: async ({ canvas }) => {
    await expect(canvas.getByRole('tablist', { name: 'Documentation' })).toBeVisible()
    const [overview, specs, guidelines] = canvas.getAllByRole('tab')
    await expect([overview, specs, guidelines].map((t) => t.textContent)).toEqual(['Overview', 'Specs', 'Guidelines'])
    // Overview first, always.
    await expect(overview).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true')
    await expect(canvas.getByRole('tabpanel')).toHaveTextContent('What it is.')
    // Mouse.
    await userEvent.click(specs)
    await waitFor(() => expect(canvas.getByRole('tabpanel')).toHaveTextContent('How it is built.'))
    // Arrow keys select as they move: a docs page, not a toolbar.
    await userEvent.keyboard('{ArrowRight}')
    await waitFor(() => expect(guidelines).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true'))
    await waitFor(() => expect(canvas.getByRole('tabpanel')).toHaveTextContent('How to use it.'))
    await userEvent.keyboard('{ArrowLeft}{ArrowLeft}')
    await waitFor(() => expect(overview).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true'))
    await expect(overview).toHaveFocus()
  },
}

const anatomy = (
  <Anatomy
    parts={[

  >
    {example}

export const AnatomyMarkers: Story = {
  name: 'Anatomy',
  render: () => anatomy,
  play: async ({ canvas }) => {
    // One marker per part, each named by number and part.
    const markers = await canvas.findAllByRole('img', { name: /^\d: / })
    await expect(markers.map((m) => m.getAttribute('aria-label'))).toEqual(['1: Container', '2: Start icon'])
    await expect(markers.map((m) => m.textContent)).toEqual(['1', '2'])
    // Each sits above its part, centred on it, with a line down to the part.
    for (const [marker, part] of [
      [markers[0], canvas.getByRole('button')],
      [markers[1], canvas.getByRole('button').querySelector('svg')!],
    ] as const) {
      const m = marker.getBoundingClientRect()
      const p = part.getBoundingClientRect()
      await expect(Math.abs(m.left + m.width / 2 - (p.left + p.width / 2))).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1)
      await expect(m.bottom).toBeLessThan(p.top)
      const line = (marker.previousElementSibling as HTMLElement).getBoundingClientRect()
      await expect(Math.abs(line.bottom - p.top)).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1)
    }
    // The key lists every part.
    const key = canvas.getByRole('table')
    await expect(within(key).getByRole('rowheader', { name: 'Start icon' })).toBeVisible()
    await expect(key).not.toHaveTextContent('Not found')
    // Backticks in a description become inline code.
    await expect(within(key).getByText('aria-hidden').tagName).toBe('CODE')
    await expect(key).not.toHaveTextContent('`')
  },
}

export const AnatomyCrowded: Story = {
  render: () => (
    <Anatomy
      parts={[
        { name: 'Container', selector: 'button' },
        { name: 'Label', selector: 'button' },
        { name: 'Again', selector: 'button' },
      ]}
    >
      {example}
    </Anatomy>
  ),
  play: async ({ canvas }) => {
    // Parts with the same centre still get three markers that do not overlap:
    // one above, one below, one slid aside.
    const boxes = (await canvas.findAllByRole('img', { name: /^\d: / })).map((m) => m.getBoundingClientRect())
    await expect(boxes).toHaveLength(3)
    for (const [i, a] of boxes.entries())
      for (const b of boxes.slice(i + 1))
        await expect(a.right <= b.left || b.right <= a.left || a.bottom <= b.top || b.bottom <= a.top).toBe(true)
  },
}

const spec = (
  <SpecTable
    caption="Measurements, md"
    rows={[
      { part: 'Container', property: 'Height', token: '--control-md' },
      { part: 'Container', property: 'Background', token: '--color-surface' },
      { part: 'Label', property: 'Line height', token: '--leading-body' },

export const Spec: Story = {
  render: () => spec,
  play: async ({ canvas }) => {
    const rows = canvas.getAllByRole('row').slice(1) as HTMLTableRowElement[]
    const value = (row: HTMLTableRowElement) => row.cells[3]
    // A length resolves to px, calc() and all.
    await expect(value(rows[0])).toHaveTextContent(/^32px$/)
    await expect(value(rows[0])).toHaveAttribute('data-kind', 'length')
    // A colour shows a swatch and the computed colour.
    const background = value(rows[1])
    await expect(background).toHaveAttribute('data-kind', 'color')
    await expect(background.querySelector('[aria-hidden="true"]')).not.toBeNull()
    // Anything else shows its declared value.
    await expect(value(rows[2])).toHaveAttribute('data-kind', 'raw')
    // The value follows the theme.
    const html = document.documentElement
    const wasDark = html.classList.contains('dark')
    const before = background.textContent
    html.classList.toggle('dark')
    try {
      await waitFor(() => expect(background.textContent).not.toBe(before))
    } finally {
      html.classList.toggle('dark', wasDark)
    }
    await waitFor(() => expect(background.textContent).toBe(before))
  },
}

export const StateRow: Story = {
  name: 'States',
  render: () => states,
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    // Storybook announces each render, and the addon rewrites the stylesheets
    // then (docs pages included). The test runner announces nothing, so play
    // Storybook's part.
    addons.getChannel().emit(STORY_RENDERED)
    const cells = within(canvasElement).getAllByRole('listitem')
    await expect(cells.map((c) => c.lastElementChild!.textContent)).toEqual(['Enabled', 'Hover', 'Focus', 'Pressed', 'Disabled'])
    const stage = (label: string) => canvasElement.querySelector<HTMLElement>(`[data-state="${label}"]`)!
    await expect(stage('Hover')).toHaveClass('pseudo-hover-all')
    await expect(stage('Focus')).toHaveClass('pseudo-focus-visible-all')
    await expect(stage('Pressed')).toHaveClass('pseudo-active-all')
    await expect(stage('Disabled').querySelector('button')).toBeDisabled()
    // The forced states actually paint: the addon rewrote :hover and friends.
    const look = (label: string) => {
      const s = getComputedStyle(stage(label).querySelector('button')!)
      return `${s.backgroundColor} ${s.outlineStyle}`
    }
    // What the addon did to the stylesheets, for the failure message.
    const rewritten = () => {
      const button = stage('Hover').querySelector('button')!
      const rules = [...document.styleSheets].flatMap((sheet) => {
        try {
          return [...sheet.cssRules]
        } catch {
          return []
        }
      })
      const hover = rules.filter((r): r is CSSStyleRule => r instanceof CSSStyleRule && r.selectorText.includes(':hover'))
      const forced = hover.filter((r) => r.selectorText.includes('pseudo-hover-all'))
      const engaged = forced.filter((r) => button.matches(r.selectorText))
      return `${document.styleSheets.length} sheets, ${hover.length} :hover rules, ${forced.length} rewritten, ${engaged.length} reach the button: ${engaged.map((r) => r.cssText).join(' | ').slice(0, 300) || hover.find((r) => r.selectorText.includes('button'))?.cssText.slice(0, 300)}`
    }
    await waitFor(() => {
      // Again on each try: a stylesheet Vite injects late is rewritten too.
      addons.getChannel().emit(STORY_RENDERED)
      expect(look('Hover'), rewritten()).not.toBe(look('Enabled'))
    })
    // No transition to wait out: each state shows its end value at once.
    await expect(getComputedStyle(stage('Hover').querySelector('button')!).transitionDuration).toBe('0s')
    await expect(look('Pressed')).not.toBe(look('Hover'))
    await expect(getComputedStyle(stage('Focus').querySelector('button')!).outlineStyle).toBe('solid')
  },
}

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import { expect } from 'storybook/test'
import { TokenTable } from './TokenTable'
import docs from './docs.module.css'

const TOKENS = [
  { name: '--focus-width', use: 'Ring thickness, on every focusable element' },
  { name: '--focus-offset', use: 'Ring outside the element: buttons, fields, links, free-standing controls' },
  { name: '--focus-offset-inset', use: 'Ring inside the element: tabs, rows, close buttons in a panel' },
]

const SAMPLE: React.CSSProperties = {
  inlineSize: 'var(--control-md)',
  blockSize: 'var(--control-md)',
  borderRadius: 'var(--radius-control)',
  background: 'var(--color-background-neutral)',
  outline: 'var(--focus-width) solid var(--color-border-focused)',
}

// Both rings drawn at rest, so the page shows the difference without a
// keyboard.
function RingDemo() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stackWide}>
      <TokenTable tokens={TOKENS} />
      <div className={docs.row}>
        <div data-ring="offset" style={{ ...SAMPLE, outlineOffset: 'var(--focus-offset)' }} />
        <span className={docs.caption}>offset</span>
        <div data-ring="inset" style={{ ...SAMPLE, outlineOffset: 'var(--focus-offset-inset)' }} />
        <span className={docs.caption}>offset-inset</span>
      </div>
    </div>
  )
}

# Focus One ring for the whole kit: `outline: var(--focus-width) solid var(--color-border-...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as FocusStories from './Focus.stories'

<Meta of={FocusStories} />

# Focus

One ring for the whole kit: `outline: var(--focus-width) solid var(--color-border-focused)`,
shown on `:focus-visible` only. Its colour is `--color-border-focused`, measured at 3:1
against the page (see [Colors](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs)).

<Canvas of={FocusStories.Rings} />

## Outside or inside

There are two offsets and the choice is mechanical.

**`--focus-offset`** draws the ring outside the element. It is the default
for anything that stands on its own: buttons, fields, links, checkboxes.

**`--focus-offset-inset`** draws it inside. Use it when the element sits
flush against the edge of a container that clips its overflow, or when an
outside ring would run into a neighbour: tabs, table rows and sortable
headers, the close button in a modal, popover, alert
or toast, the remove button in a tag, the steppers in a number input.

A third value is a smell. The one exception is a selected colour swatch,
which already carries a selection ring at `--focus-offset`, so its focus
ring sits one pixel further out to stay visible.

## Why the ring is in pixels

`--focus-width` and both offsets are plain pixels, not `rem`. A ring is a
stroke, and WCAG 2.4.13 measures it in CSS pixels.

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import { expect, waitFor } from 'storybook/test'
import { Button } from '@/components/buttons/Button'
import { anatomyPartFor, startInspector, type TokenValue } from './inspect'

/**
 * What the Specs tab draws inside the preview frame: the parts numbered, the
 * hovered row's redline, and the tokens resolved as the frame sees them.
 */
const meta = {
  title: 'Site/Inspect',
  render: () => <Button>Subscribe</Button>,
} satisfies Meta

export default meta
type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

const layer = () => document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[data-playground-inspector]')

/** Which anatomy part a Specs row is about. */
export const RowToPart: Story = {
  play: async () => {
    const names = ['Container', 'Start icon', 'Label', 'Title', 'Previous month']
    await expect(anatomyPartFor('Container, outlined', names)).toBe('Container')
    await expect(anatomyPartFor('Title and description', names)).toBe('Title')
    await expect(anatomyPartFor('Icon', names)).toBe('Start icon')
    await expect(anatomyPartFor('Previous and next', names)).toBe('Previous month')
    await expect(anatomyPartFor('Focus ring', names)).toBe('Focus ring')
    // A whole word only: "Lab" is not Label.
    await expect(anatomyPartFor('Lab', names)).toBeNull()
    await expect(anatomyPartFor('Option', names)).toBeNull()
  },
}

export const Default: Story = {
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    let values: Record<string, TokenValue> = {}
    const inspector = startInspector(
      () => canvasElement,
      (v) => (values = v),
    )
    const parts = [
      { name: 'Container', selector: 'button' },
      { name: 'Missing', selector: 'nav' },
    ]
    try {
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: ['--control-md', '--color-background-brand-bold', '--nope'] })
      // One number, on the part that is there; decoration only.
      await waitFor(() => expect(layer()?.textContent).toBe('①'))
      await expect(layer()).toHaveAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true')
      await expect(getComputedStyle(layer()!).pointerEvents).toBe('none')
      await waitFor(() => expect(values['--control-md']).toEqual({ kind: 'length', text: '32px' }))
      await expect(values['--color-background-brand-bold'].kind).toBe('color')
      await expect(values['--nope']).toEqual({ kind: 'missing', text: 'Not defined here' })

      // A row's redline: the part's height, with its value.
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: ['--control-md'], highlight: { part: 'Container', property: 'Height', token: '--control-md' } })
      await waitFor(() => expect(layer()?.textContent).toContain('Height 32px'))
      const button = canvasElement.querySelector('button')!.getBoundingClientRect()
      const line = [...layer()!.children].find((el) => (el as HTMLElement).style.width === '1px') as HTMLElement
      await expect(parseFloat(line.style.height)).toBeCloseTo(button.height, 0)

      // Inline padding shades the two sides.
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: [], highlight: { part: 'Container', property: 'Inline padding', token: '--x' } })
      await waitFor(() => expect([...layer()!.children].filter((el) => (el as HTMLElement).style.background.includes('0.25'))).toHaveLength(2))

      // The focus ring at its width and offset around the focusable element, though no anatomy part names it.
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: ['--focus-width'], highlight: { part: 'Focus ring', property: 'Width', token: '--focus-width' } })
      await waitFor(() => expect(layer()?.textContent).toContain('Width 2px'))
      const ring = [...layer()!.children].find((el) => (el as HTMLElement).style.borderWidth === '2px') as HTMLElement
      await expect(parseFloat(ring.style.width)).toBeCloseTo(button.width + 2 * (2 + 2), 0)

      // Radius marks the corner; font size shades the first line of text.
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: [], highlight: { part: 'Container', property: 'Corner radius', token: '--x' } })
      await waitFor(() => expect([...layer()!.children].some((el) => (el as HTMLElement).style.borderTopLeftRadius !== '')).toBe(true))
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: [], highlight: { part: 'Container', property: 'Font size', token: '--x' } })
      await waitFor(() => expect([...layer()!.children].filter((el) => (el as HTMLElement).style.background.includes('0.25'))).toHaveLength(1))

      // A forced state goes on the item's root as the pseudo-states addon's class, and comes off.
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: [], pseudo: 'hover' })
      await expect(canvasElement).toHaveClass('pseudo-hover-all')
      inspector.set({ parts, tokens: [], pseudo: 'active' })
      await expect(canvasElement).not.toHaveClass('pseudo-hover-all')
      await expect(canvasElement).toHaveClass('pseudo-active-all')
    } finally {
      inspector.set(null)
    }
    await expect(layer()).toBeNull()
    await expect(canvasElement).not.toHaveClass('pseudo-active-all')
  },
}

# Layering Four layers for everything that leaves the page flow. A component picks the lay...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as LayeringStories from './Layering.stories'

<Meta of={LayeringStories} />

# Layering

Four layers for everything that leaves the page flow. A component picks
the layer by what it is, never by trying a bigger number.

<Canvas of={LayeringStories.Layers} />

## One layer for every overlay

Popovers, menus, listboxes, date pickers and modals all share
`--layer-overlay`. They are portalled to the end of `<body>`, so at an equal
z-index the one opened last paints on top: a Select opened inside a Modal
lands above the Modal without either knowing about the other. Giving the
Modal a higher layer would break exactly that case.

Tooltips sit one layer up because they can belong to anything, including a
trigger inside an open overlay. Toasts sit above everything: a toast raised
while a modal is open still has to be read.

## Local z-index

A value used only to order parts inside one component (a table's sticky
header at `1`, the tab indicator at `-1`) is local and stays a plain number.
Keep these at single digits so they stay well below `--layer-sticky`.

# Motion Three transition durations and one spinner speed. Every `transition` in the kit r...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as MotionStories from './Motion.stories'

<Meta of={MotionStories} />

# Motion

Three transition durations and one spinner speed. Every `transition` in the
kit reads one of them; nothing types a number of milliseconds.

<Canvas of={MotionStories.Durations} />

## Choosing a step

The step follows what moves, not how important it is. A popup appearing
is `fast`: it answers a click, and anything slower reads as lag. A colour
or state change is `base`. Something that travels across the screen (the
tab indicator, a toast, a progress bar's fill) is `slow`, because the eye has to follow
it. If a new transition does not fit one of the three, that is a reason to
question the transition before adding a fourth step.

Easing is the browser default (`ease`) except where something grows or
shrinks: Collapse opens with `ease-out`, so the panel arrives
fast and settles. There is no easing token: two curves, each with an
obvious owner, do not need a name yet.

## Reduced motion

Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the three transition steps resolve to
`0ms` in `tokens.css`, so every transition in the kit stops in one place
without each component repeating a media query.

Two things are exempt. Toast swaps its slide for a 200ms fade, written as
a number on purpose, since the tokens would turn the fade into a jump.
And spinners: a stopped spinner says nothing is happening, so instead of
stopping they slow from `--duration-spin` to `--duration-spin-reduced`.
Each spinner opts into that itself.

Loop animations with their own rhythm (the skeleton pulse, the
indeterminate progress bar) keep their own timing: they are a single
animation each, not a step anyone else should reuse.

} satisfies Meta

export default meta
type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>

const wrapper = (canvasElement: HTMLElement) => canvasElement.querySelector('[data-preview-theme]')

export const Dark: Story = {
  globals: { appearance: 'dark' },
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {
    await expect(wrapper(canvasElement)).toHaveClass('dark')
    // Popups portal to <body>: the frame's <html> goes dark with it.
    await expect(document.documentElement).toHaveClass('dark')
  },
}

  globals: { appearance: 'light' },

    await expect(document.documentElement).not.toHaveClass('dark')
  },
}

  globals: { appearance: 'system' },
  beforeEach: withPrefersDark(true),
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => {

}

    await expect(scope).toHaveAttribute('data-gray', 'slate')
    await expect(scope.style.getPropertyValue('--radius-factor')).toBe('1.5')
    await expect(scope.style.getPropertyValue('--radius-full')).toBe('9999px')
    // Popups portal to <body>: the frame's <html> wears the same.
    await expect(document.documentElement).toHaveAttribute('data-accent', 'rose')
    await expect(document.documentElement.style.getPropertyValue('--radius-factor')).toBe('1.5')
  },

    const scope = wrapper(canvasElement) as HTMLElement
    await expect(scope.style.getPropertyValue('--font-sans')).toContain('Inter')
    // Headings follow: --font-heading derives from --font-sans on every element.

    await expect(getComputedStyle(text).getPropertyValue('--font-heading')).toContain('Inter')
